History & culture

The bottle and the cork: a history

From amphorae and barrels to the glass bottle and the cork stopper: how the way wine was stored transformed its trade, its ageing and the way it is drunk.

Today it is hard to imagine wine without a glass bottle closed with a stopper. Yet for most of its history wine was stored and transported in other containers, and the combination of bottle and cork that seems natural to us only became widespread in the last three centuries. That apparently modest innovation changed the way wine was traded, made long ageing possible and lies at the root of the modern idea of the vintage.

Amphorae, wineskins and barrels

In antiquity, wine was kept in large earthenware jars and transported in amphorae, ceramic vessels that could be sealed with stoppers of clay, wood or even cork, sometimes coated with resin or pitch. Leather wineskins were also used for overland transport and everyday drinking. Glass was known, and in Roman times jugs and cups of blown glass were made, but it was an expensive, fragile material, better suited to serving than to storing or shipping.

The wooden barrel, of Celtic or Gaulish origin, gradually replaced amphorae in the northern Roman Empire and became, in the Middle Ages, the main container for the European wine trade. Wine travelled in bulk in casks and was sold by the jug in taverns and homes. This had a drawback: once a cask was broached, contact with air spoiled the wine quickly. Most wines were drunk young, within the year.

English glass

A decisive technical change took place in England in the seventeenth century. A shortage of wood led to its replacement by coal as fuel in glass furnaces. The higher temperatures made it possible to produce thicker, darker and stronger glass. Sir Kenelm Digby, a versatile figure of the time, is often credited with an important role in developing these sturdy bottles, although the exact contribution of each inventor is hard to establish.

The first bottles of this kind had bulbous shapes, sometimes called onion bottles, which stood upright only with difficulty. They were used mainly to carry wine from the cask to the table. Over the eighteenth century their shape gradually lengthened until it became cylindrical. This change had an enormous consequence: the bottle could be stored lying down.

Cork and the bottle on its side

Cork is the bark of the cork oak, Quercus suber, a tree native to the western Mediterranean. It is harvested without felling the tree, which regrows its bark after several years. It is light, elastic and impermeable, and it compresses and expands to fit the neck of the bottle. Portugal and Spain have traditionally been the main producers.

Although cork was already known in antiquity, its systematic use to close wine bottles became widespread from the seventeenth century. At first stoppers protruded from the neck so they could be pulled out by hand. When they began to be driven fully into the neck, a tool was needed to extract them: the corkscrew, which appears in English sources of the seventeenth century and gave rise to many patents, such as the one obtained by the Reverend Samuel Henshall in 1795.

Storing the bottle on its side keeps the cork moist and in contact with the wine, so it does not dry out or let air in. This created the possibility of ageing wine in bottle for years or decades, with a slow, reductive evolution very different from what happens in barrel.

Consequences for wine

The combination of cylindrical bottle and cork had far-reaching effects:

  • It allowed wines for laying down to be valued and gave vintages commercial importance.
  • It made possible the development of wines such as Vintage Port, designed to improve over many years in bottle.
  • It made modern sparkling wine possible, since the gas from a second fermentation required a strong container and an airtight closure. The legend that credits Dom Pérignon with bringing the cork to Champagne is unproven.
  • It encouraged producers to bottle their own wine and identify it with a label, rather than selling it in bulk.

For sparkling wine, the stopper had to be held in place to withstand the pressure; string was used at first, then wire. The modern wire cage, the muselet, became standard in the nineteenth century.

Industrialisation and standardisation

For centuries bottles were blown by hand, so their shape and capacity varied. Moulds were introduced in the nineteenth century and, at the beginning of the twentieth, automatic bottle-making machines, which made production cheaper and sizes more uniform. Over time each region settled on its characteristic shapes, such as the high-shouldered Bordeaux bottle, the sloping-shouldered Burgundy bottle or the tall, slender Rhine bottle. In the European Union, 75 centilitres became the standard capacity for still wine.

New closures

Cork has a well-known problem: in a small proportion of bottles it can give the wine musty or damp-cardboard smells, caused mainly by the compound TCA (2,4,6-trichloroanisole). This fault, known as cork taint, spurred the search for alternatives in the last decades of the twentieth century.

Synthetic stoppers appeared, as did technical stoppers made from treated agglomerated cork and, above all, the screwcap. In the early twenty-first century, groups of producers in Australia's Clare Valley and in New Zealand collectively adopted screwcaps for their wines, especially for aromatic whites such as Riesling and Sauvignon Blanc. Today screwcaps dominate in some countries, while in others natural cork is still preferred, particularly for wines meant for ageing. The cork industry, for its part, has developed methods to reduce the presence of TCA.

An object with a history

The bottle and its closure are much more than packaging. Their evolution made possible the trade in bottled wine, long ageing and the birth of entire styles. That is why the history of modern wine is, to a large extent, also the history of glass and cork.
